label: Formulating an optimization problem
lesson:
# Formulating an optimization problem

Every EDA engine is an optimizer wearing a domain costume. A placer, a sizer, a router and a scheduler each choose values for some unknowns to make a cost small while respecting rules. Writing that down precisely, as decision variables, an objective and constraints, is the first act of tool design. A sloppy formulation produces a fast solver for the wrong problem, and most QoR surprises trace back to what was, or was not, written into the model.

## Decision variables versus data

Decision variables are the quantities the optimizer is free to set. Everything else is data. In gate sizing the variables are the size of each cell; the library, the netlist and the clock period are data. In global placement the variables are the $(x, y)$ coordinates of movable cells; pad positions and the die outline are data. Derived quantities such as arrival times are neither: they are functions of the variables computed by the timer.

The encoding matters as much as the choice. An HLS scheduler can use one integer start time per operation, or binaries $x_{i,t} = 1$ when operation $i$ starts in cycle $t$. The binary, time-indexed form makes per-cycle resource limits linear, $\sum_i x_{i,t} \le a$, which an ILP solver can use. A macro that may rotate gets one binary that swaps its width and height. Pick variables so that the rules become simple functions of them.

## Objective versus constraints

The objective is what we trade; the constraints are what we must meet. A buffering tool must meet required times and wants little buffer area, so it minimizes area subject to timing at every endpoint. Swapping the roles, minimizing slack subject to an area cap, is a different problem with a different answer.

A constraint can be made soft by moving it into the objective with a weight: a placer that minimizes $W(x) + \lambda D(x)$ treats density $D$ as a penalty rather than a hard bin capacity. Then the optimizer may buy wirelength with overflow, and a router scoring wirelength plus 1000 times overflow can legitimately return 3 units of overflow if that saves enough wire. A worst-case objective such as worst negative slack, $\max_p \ell_p$, is written with an auxiliary variable: minimize $t$ subject to $t \ge \ell_p$ for every path $p$. That epigraph trick keeps a linear model linear.

## Proxies, scaling and infeasibility

Most EDA objectives are proxies. Placers minimize half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL) although the real metric is routed length; sizers use Elmore or table delays although signoff uses a full timer. The gap between proxy and signoff is a design decision to be measured, not ignored.

Scaling is the second trap. If delay is about 200 ps and area about 10,000 square microns, the objective $\text{delay} + \text{area}$ is almost all area, and timing is ignored. Normalize each term, for example by its baseline value, before choosing weights.

Infeasibility is a property of the constraints alone. If a clock-tree model has no feasible point, look for conflicting constraints, such as a skew bound tighter than wire delays allow; the objective plays no part. Finally, two formulations with the same optimum can have very different relaxations, and the tighter one solves faster.

## Going deeper

Boyd and Vandenberghe, "Convex Optimization" (2004), chapter 4 on problem forms and equivalent reformulations; Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design: From Graph Partitioning to Timing Closure" (2nd ed., 2022), which states each physical-design step as an optimization problem.

problems.q:
An HLS scheduler assigns operations to clock cycles under a resource limit. Which encoding of the decision makes an ILP possible?

A) A binary per pair of resources

B) A binary $x_{i,t}$ that is 1 when operation i starts in cycle t

C) A real number per operation equal to its delay

D) One integer for the total latency only
problems.a: A binary $x_{i,t}$ that is 1 when operation i starts in cycle t
problems.e: Time-indexed binaries let both precedence and per-cycle resource limits be written as linear constraints.

problems.q:
In global placement, which quantity is a decision variable rather than data?

A) The netlist connectivity

B) The (x, y) location of each movable cell

C) The die outline

D) The positions of fixed I/O pads
problems.a: The (x, y) location of each movable cell
problems.e: The placer sets movable-cell coordinates. Connectivity, pad positions and the die are inputs the formulation must respect.

problems.q:
An HLS scheduler assigns operations to clock cycles under a resource limit. Which encoding of the decision makes an ILP possible?

A) A real number per operation equal to its delay

B) A binary per pair of resources

C) One integer for the total latency only

D) A binary $x_{i,t}$ that is 1 when operation i starts in cycle t
problems.a: A binary $x_{i,t}$ that is 1 when operation i starts in cycle t
problems.e: Time-indexed binaries let both precedence and per-cycle resource limits be written as linear constraints.

problems.q:
Timing-driven placement wants to reduce the worst negative slack. Written as an optimization, what is the cleanest objective form?

A) Minimize the clock period with no other constraint

B) Maximize the number of paths

C) Minimize the product of all slacks

D) Minimize t subject to t greater than or equal to each path's lateness
problems.a: Minimize t subject to t greater than or equal to each path's lateness
problems.e: A max of terms is linearized with an auxiliary variable t bounded below by every term: an epigraph formulation.

problems.q:
A buffering tool must meet every endpoint's required time and use as little buffer area as possible. How should it be formulated?

A) Minimize the sum of arrival times with no constraints

B) Minimize worst slack subject to an area limit

C) Minimize buffer area subject to timing constraints at every endpoint

D) Maximize buffer count subject to an area limit
problems.a: Minimize buffer area subject to timing constraints at every endpoint
problems.e: Meeting timing is a hard requirement, so it is a constraint; area is what we trade, so it is the objective.

problems.q:
A buffering tool must meet every endpoint's required time and use as little buffer area as possible. How should it be formulated?

A) Minimize buffer area subject to timing constraints at every endpoint

B) Minimize worst slack subject to an area limit

C) Minimize the sum of arrival times with no constraints

D) Maximize buffer count subject to an area limit
problems.a: Minimize buffer area subject to timing constraints at every endpoint
problems.e: Meeting timing is a hard requirement, so it is a constraint; area is what we trade, so it is the objective.

problems.q:
A sizing objective sums delay in ps and area in square microns with weights 1 and 1. Area values are around 10,000 while delays are around 200. What happens?

A) Delay dominates because it is listed first

B) Area dominates the objective, so the optimizer nearly ignores timing

C) The optimizer rejects mixed units

D) The two terms are balanced automatically
problems.a: Area dominates the objective, so the optimizer nearly ignores timing
problems.e: Weights must account for scale. Without normalization the larger-magnitude term controls the trade-off.

problems.q:
A placer optimizes HPWL, but the final metric is routed wirelength after detailed routing. What is this a case of?

A) A constraint violation

B) A decision variable error

C) Optimizing a tractable proxy of the true objective

D) A nonconvex constraint
problems.a: Optimizing a tractable proxy of the true objective
problems.e: Most EDA objectives are proxies (HPWL for routed length, Elmore for signoff delay); the gap between proxy and signoff metric must be tracked.

problems.q:
A placer optimizes HPWL, but the final metric is routed wirelength after detailed routing. What is this a case of?

A) A nonconvex constraint

B) Optimizing a tractable proxy of the true objective

C) A decision variable error

D) A constraint violation
problems.a: Optimizing a tractable proxy of the true objective
problems.e: Most EDA objectives are proxies (HPWL for routed length, Elmore for signoff delay); the gap between proxy and signoff metric must be tracked.

label: Continuous versus combinatorial optimization
lesson:
# Continuous versus combinatorial optimization

Once the variables are fixed, the problem falls into a class: linear, quadratic, convex, integer, mixed-integer, nonconvex, combinatorial or black-box. The class decides which algorithms apply, what guarantees exist and how the run time scales. EDA uses every class, often in sequence: a continuous relaxation for global structure, then a combinatorial repair. Recognizing the class of a subproblem is how a tool designer chooses between a sparse linear solve, an ILP solver, a dynamic program and a local search.

## Counting a discrete decision space

A combinatorial problem has a finite but enormous set of candidate solutions, and its size is the first thing to compute. If each of $n$ gates picks one of $k$ sizes independently, there are $k^n$ sizings: 10 gates with 3 sizes give $3^{10} = 59049$. Assigning $n$ cells to $n$ legal slots is a permutation, $n!$ of them: $8! = 40320$. Splitting $n$ cells into two unlabeled halves of $n/2$ gives $\binom{n}{n/2}/2$ bisections, because swapping the halves gives the same split: 8 cells give $70/2 = 35$.

The classic slips are confusing $k^n$ with $n^k$, forgetting that halves are unlabeled, or counting subsets ($2^n$) when the sizes are fixed. These counts grow exponentially or factorially, so a few dozen variables already put exhaustive search out of reach. The space is also unstructured: there is no gradient between two permutations.

## Naming the problem class

Read the class off the variables, objective and constraints. Continuous variables with a linear objective and linear constraints give a linear program (LP). Add a convex quadratic objective and it is a quadratic program (QP): quadratic placement, $\min \sum w_{ij}(x_i - x_j)^2$ with some cells fixed, is an unconstrained convex QP solved by one sparse linear system. Binary selection with linear covering rows, such as choosing test patterns to cover all faults, is a 0-1 integer linear program (ILP). Mixing continuous coordinates with binary relative-position variables, as in big-M floorplanning, is a mixed-integer linear program (MILP).

Continuous sizing with posynomial Elmore delays is a geometric program, convex after the substitution $x = e^u$. A constraint $(x_i - x_j)^2 + (y_i - y_j)^2 \ge d^2$ describes the outside of a disk, so it makes the model a nonconvex quadratically constrained program (QCQP).

## Why EDA alternates continuous and discrete

Legal placement is discrete (cells on rows and sites), but global placers solve a continuous relaxation first because gradients and sparse solvers scale to millions of cells. Legalization then repairs the small discrete violations. Continuous sizing returns values like 2.37x for a library of 1x, 2x, 4x and 8x, so a discretization step snaps sizes and repairs the timing that rounding breaks.

Some problems stay combinatorial: detailed routing chooses paths on a discrete track grid, and technology mapping chooses matches that cover a subject graph, solved exactly on trees by dynamic programming. Others are black boxes: tuning ten flow knobs where each evaluation is a six-hour run with no gradient calls for surrogate-based search. The structural difference for the designer is simple. Continuous problems offer gradients and local models; discrete ones need enumeration, bounds, relaxations or neighborhoods.

## Going deeper

Papadimitriou and Steiglitz, "Combinatorial Optimization: Algorithms and Complexity" (1982), chapter 1; Boyd and Vandenberghe, "Convex Optimization" (2004), chapter 4 for the LP, QP, QCQP and geometric-program forms.

problems.q:
A detailed placer assigns 4 cells to 4 legal slots, one cell per slot. How many assignments are possible?

A) 256

B) 25

C) 16

D) 24
problems.e: An assignment is a permutation, so there are $4! = 24$. This is a combinatorial problem: no gradient exists between permutations.

problems.q:
A partitioner splits 4 cells into two unlabeled halves of 2 cells each. How many bisections are there?

A) 8

B) 3

C) 6

D) 16
problems.e: Choose the 2 cells of one half, $\binom{4}{2} = 6$, then divide by 2 because swapping the halves gives the same bisection: 3.

problems.q:
A partitioner splits 10 cells into two unlabeled halves of 5 cells each. How many bisections are there?

A) 512

B) 252

C) 126

D) 1024
problems.e: Choose the 5 cells of one half, $\binom{10}{5} = 252$, then divide by 2 because swapping the halves gives the same bisection: 126.

problems.q:
Minimize $\sum w_{ij}(x_i - x_j)^2$ over real cell coordinates, with some coordinates fixed. What class of problem is this?

A) A linear program

B) An unconstrained convex quadratic program

C) A nonconvex QCQP

D) An integer linear program
problems.a: An unconstrained convex quadratic program
problems.e: The objective is a positive semidefinite quadratic in continuous variables with no inequality constraints; solving it is one sparse linear system.

problems.q:
Which problem is a mixed-integer linear program?

A) Quadratic placement with fixed pads

B) Floorplanning with continuous block coordinates and binary relative-position variables in linear non-overlap constraints

C) Gradient descent on wirelength

D) Computing an Elmore delay
problems.a: Floorplanning with continuous block coordinates and binary relative-position variables in linear non-overlap constraints
problems.e: It mixes continuous coordinates with binaries and keeps every constraint linear through big-M terms.

problems.q:
Gate sizing with continuous sizes and Elmore-style delays written as posynomials is which kind of problem?

A) A nonconvex problem with no convex form

B) A geometric program, convex after a log change of variables

C) An integer program

D) A linear program in the sizes
problems.a: A geometric program, convex after a log change of variables
problems.e: Posynomial objectives and constraints become convex in log variables, which is why continuous sizing (as in TILOS-era work) has global optima.

problems.q:
A continuous optimizer returns sizes like 2.37x for a library offering 1x, 2x, 4x and 8x. What step remains?

A) Discretization: snap to library sizes and repair the timing that rounding breaks

B) Rerun the same continuous solve

C) Nothing: tools accept fractional sizes

D) Change the netlist
problems.a: Discretization: snap to library sizes and repair the timing that rounding breaks
problems.e: Continuous sizing is a relaxation of the discrete library choice; rounding can violate constraints, so a repair or local search follows.

problems.q:
A continuous optimizer returns sizes like 2.37x for a library offering 1x, 2x, 4x and 8x. What step remains?

A) Rerun the same continuous solve

B) Change the netlist

C) Nothing: tools accept fractional sizes

D) Discretization: snap to library sizes and repair the timing that rounding breaks
problems.a: Discretization: snap to library sizes and repair the timing that rounding breaks
problems.e: Continuous sizing is a relaxation of the discrete library choice; rounding can violate constraints, so a repair or local search follows.

problems.q:
A continuous optimizer returns sizes like 2.37x for a library offering 1x, 2x, 4x and 8x. What step remains?

A) Rerun the same continuous solve

B) Nothing: tools accept fractional sizes

C) Change the netlist

D) Discretization: snap to library sizes and repair the timing that rounding breaks
problems.a: Discretization: snap to library sizes and repair the timing that rounding breaks
problems.e: Continuous sizing is a relaxation of the discrete library choice; rounding can violate constraints, so a repair or local search follows.

label: Why exact optimization is hard
lesson:
# Why exact optimization is hard

Most EDA problems worth solving are NP-hard: partitioning, floorplanning, placement, routing, covering, scheduling under resources. That is not a reason to give up but a statement about which promises a tool can make. Hardness tells the designer to expect heuristics, bounds and decomposition, to measure quality against baselines, and to look for structure in real instances that the worst case ignores.

## How fast enumeration runs out

Exhaustive search is the honest baseline, and arithmetic shows why it fails. Sizing 60 gates with 2 sizes each has $2^{60} \approx 10^{18.1}$ configurations. At $10^{9}$ evaluations per second, enumeration takes about $10^{9}$ seconds, roughly 37 years. With 100 gates it is about $10^{21}$ seconds, far beyond the age of the universe, about $4 \times 10^{17}$ seconds.

The computation is in logarithms: $\log_{10} k^n = n \log_{10} k$, and for orderings $\log_{10} n!$ (Stirling's formula, or a log-gamma function). Subtract the log of the evaluation rate to get the log of the time in seconds. Each extra gate multiplies the time by $k$, so faster hardware buys only a few more variables. The lesson is that any exact method must avoid visiting most of the space, which is what bounds, propagation and dynamic programming do.

## What NP-hardness does and does not say

NP-hardness is a worst-case statement: unless P equals NP, no algorithm solves every instance optimally in polynomial time. It does not say every instance is hard, and it does not forbid exact solvers on small or structured instances. Two-coloring a conflict graph is a linear-time bipartiteness check, while three-coloring, as in triple-patterning decomposition, is NP-complete; tools therefore split the graph into small components and solve those exactly or heuristically.

Integer programs are the common trap. Each LP relaxation in branch and bound may solve in seconds, yet the number of nodes can grow exponentially. Convexity is the property that usually makes continuous problems tractable, since every local optimum is then global. Nonconvex continuous problems can have many local optima, and descent finds only the one whose basin it starts in. Structure, such as planarity or small treewidth, can make restricted versions easy.

## Engineering under hardness

Production engines promise good solutions in bounded run time, usually without an optimality certificate, and are judged against QoR baselines. Where a certificate exists it is valuable: a MILP solver's gap between incumbent and best bound says how far the answer can be from optimal, so a flow can stop at 1% and know the price.

Run-time scaling is measured as carefully as quality. If a partitioner takes 1 s at $10^4$ cells and 100 s at $10^5$, its empirical complexity is about $n^2$, hopeless at $10^7$ cells. Multilevel methods answer by coarsening the netlist, solving the small clustered problem, and refining level by level. Relaxation gives bounds, decomposition gives smaller problems, and approximation algorithms give worst-case ratios: greedy set cover is within about $\ln n$ of optimal. These three moves, plus search, are the toolkit the next concept organizes.

## Going deeper

Garey and Johnson, "Computers and Intractability" (1979), for NP-completeness and the classic hard problems; Karypis and Kumar's papers on multilevel hypergraph partitioning (hMETIS) for the coarsen-solve-refine pattern.

problems.q:
An exhaustive optimizer evaluates $10^{7}$ configurations per second. Roughly how long does it take to enumerate all $2^{36}$ sizings of 36 gates with 2 sizes each?

A) About $10^{1}$ seconds

B) About $10^{3}$ seconds

C) About $10^{6}$ seconds

D) About $10^{-4}$ seconds

E) About $10^{10}$ seconds
problems.a: About $10^{3}$ seconds
problems.e: The space has about $10^{10.8}$ points; dividing by $10^{7}$ per second leaves about $10^{3}$ seconds. For scale, the age of the universe is about $4 \times 10^{17}$ seconds.

problems.q:
An exhaustive optimizer evaluates $10^{7}$ configurations per second. Roughly how long does it take to enumerate all $19!$ orderings of 19 cells in a row?

A) About $10^{17}$ seconds

B) About $10^{13}$ seconds

C) About $10^{10}$ seconds

D) About $10^{5}$ seconds

E) About $10^{3}$ seconds
problems.a: About $10^{10}$ seconds
problems.e: The space has about $10^{17.1}$ points; dividing by $10^{7}$ per second leaves about $10^{10}$ seconds. For scale, the age of the universe is about $4 \times 10^{17}$ seconds.

problems.q:
An exhaustive optimizer evaluates $10^{8}$ configurations per second. Roughly how long does it take to enumerate all $4^{80}$ sizings of 80 gates with 4 sizes each?

A) About $10^{43}$ seconds

B) About $10^{48}$ seconds

C) About $10^{40}$ seconds

D) About $10^{32}$ seconds

E) About $10^{20}$ seconds
problems.a: About $10^{40}$ seconds
problems.e: The space has about $10^{48.2}$ points; dividing by $10^{8}$ per second leaves about $10^{40}$ seconds. For scale, the age of the universe is about $4 \times 10^{17}$ seconds.

problems.q:
Which property usually makes a continuous optimization problem tractable to solve to global optimality?

A) Being smooth but nonconvex

B) Having many variables

C) Convexity of the objective and the feasible set

D) Having integer variables
problems.a: Convexity of the objective and the feasible set
problems.e: For a convex problem every local optimum is global, and interior-point and first-order methods have polynomial guarantees.

problems.q:
A problem is NP-hard in general but the instances a router sees are planar with small degree. What is the right conclusion?

A) NP-hardness disappears for planar graphs in all problems

B) The router must use brute force

C) The instances are guaranteed to be hard

D) Structure may allow exact or near-exact methods on those instances; hardness is a worst-case statement
problems.a: Structure may allow exact or near-exact methods on those instances; hardness is a worst-case statement
problems.e: Restricted classes can be easy (some problems become polynomial on planar or bounded-treewidth graphs), so structure should be exploited.

problems.q:
Why is 2-coloring a conflict graph easy while 3-coloring (as in triple patterning lithography decomposition) is hard?

A) 2-colorability is a bipartiteness check in linear time; 3-colorability is NP-complete

B) Both are NP-complete

C) 3-coloring is easy and 2-coloring is hard

D) Both are linear time
problems.a: 2-colorability is a bipartiteness check in linear time; 3-colorability is NP-complete
problems.e: A breadth-first search decides 2-coloring; 3-coloring is a classic NP-complete problem, which is why TPL decomposition uses heuristics or ILP on small components.

problems.q:
Why does a MILP solver's reported gap matter in an EDA flow?

A) It measures the runtime

B) It bounds how far the returned solution can be from optimal, so the flow can stop early with a known guarantee

C) It shows the LP is infeasible

D) It is the number of integer variables
problems.a: It bounds how far the returned solution can be from optimal, so the flow can stop early with a known guarantee
problems.e: The gap between incumbent and best bound is a certificate; stopping at 1% gap saves enormous time for a known loss.

problems.q:
Why do multilevel partitioners and placers coarsen the netlist first?

A) Coarsening is required for legality

B) Coarsening makes the problem convex

C) Solving a much smaller clustered problem gives a good global structure cheaply, refined level by level

D) Coarsening removes all local optima
problems.a: Solving a much smaller clustered problem gives a good global structure cheaply, refined level by level
problems.e: Multilevel methods decompose by scale: global decisions on few clusters, local refinement on many cells.

problems.q:
Given NP-hardness, what do production EDA engines typically promise about solution quality?

A) Random solutions

B) Good solutions in bounded runtime, often with no optimality certificate

C) Optimality whenever the design is small

D) Provably optimal solutions on every design
problems.a: Good solutions in bounded runtime, often with no optimality certificate
problems.e: Engines trade optimality for scalability, and quality is measured by benchmarks and QoR baselines rather than proofs.

label: Relax, decompose, approximate or search
lesson:
# Relax, decompose, approximate or search

Faced with an NP-hard model, a tool designer has four moves: relax a hard constraint to get a bound and a starting point, decompose the problem into smaller coupled pieces, approximate by rounding or a simpler model, or search the discrete space directly. Every major EDA engine is a recognizable combination of these moves, and naming the combination tells you what the engine can guarantee, where it will fail, and which knob to turn when it does.

## Relaxation and its bound

A relaxation enlarges the feasible set so the problem becomes easy. Replacing $x \in \{0, 1\}$ by $0 \le x \le 1$ turns an ILP into an LP. Dropping overlap and site constraints turns placement into a quadratic or smooth program. Because the relaxed set contains every feasible point, the relaxed optimum bounds the original: a lower bound for minimization.

Relaxation is rarely the end. Quadratic placement relaxes overlap and then spreads and legalizes. LP-based global routing relaxes integrality and then rounds the fractional route choices. Lagrangian relaxation is a different flavour: it moves the coupling constraints, such as timing, into the objective with multipliers, so the relaxed problem separates into per-gate subproblems. In every case a repair or coordination step must restore feasibility, and the bound tells you how much quality might remain.

## Decomposition and coordination

Decomposition splits one large problem into smaller ones. Min-cut placement recursively bisects the netlist and the die, so each region becomes an independent smaller problem. Hierarchical flows optimize blocks separately against budgets and then the top level against block abstracts. The risk is coupling: cross-block timing or congestion can be missed unless budgets are good or the levels iterate.

Formal decompositions coordinate the pieces through duality. Benders decomposition keeps the complicating integer decisions in a master problem and returns cuts from an LP subproblem's dual. ADMM splits an objective across partitions that share boundary variables and drives the copies to agree with scaled dual variables. Lagrangian relaxation, seen from this side, is price-based coordination: the multipliers are prices on shared resources. Decomposition is exact only when the coupling is handled exactly, so measure what the split costs on reference designs.

## Search, approximation and certificates

Search explores the discrete space directly with moves and an acceptance rule: simulated annealing on Polish expressions for floorplans, Fiduccia-Mattheyses passes for partitioning, local swaps in detailed placement. Search scales and adapts to odd constraints but carries no certificate. Approximation rounds or simplifies with a guarantee or at least a known error: randomized rounding of an LP, a greedy cover, an Elmore model in place of a full timer.

Exact methods survive where structure allows. Van Ginneken's buffer insertion on a routing tree and tree-covering technology mapping are dynamic programs that are optimal for their models. A strong practical pairing is search for the solution plus a relaxation for the bound: any feasible point gives an upper bound for minimization, the relaxation gives a lower bound, and the gap between them is the certificate. When a requirement such as $10^6$-cell detailed placement in minutes rules out exact methods, that pairing still tells the user what is being left on the table.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapters 2 to 5 for partition, floorplan, placement and routing strategies; Bertsekas, "Nonlinear Programming" (3rd ed., 2016), chapter on duality and decomposition.

problems.q:
Which is a relaxation of a 0-1 ILP?

A) Branching on a fractional variable

B) Fixing some variables to 1

C) Adding a cutting plane

D) Replacing $x \in \{0, 1\}$ with $0 \le x \le 1$
problems.a: Replacing $x \in \{0, 1\}$ with $0 \le x \le 1$
problems.e: A relaxation enlarges the feasible set, so its optimum bounds the original from the optimistic side.

problems.q:
Lagrangian-relaxation gate sizing moves the timing constraints into the objective with multipliers. What is gained?

A) The problem becomes integer

B) The solution is always infeasible

C) The relaxed problem separates into easy per-gate subproblems

D) Timing is ignored entirely
problems.a: The relaxed problem separates into easy per-gate subproblems
problems.e: Dualizing coupling constraints decouples the gates; multipliers coordinate them through iteration.

problems.q:
A global router solves the LP relaxation of its ILP and then rounds the fractional route choices. Which strategy pair is this?

A) Decomposition followed by enumeration

B) Relaxation followed by approximation (rounding)

C) Search followed by dynamic programming

D) Pure exhaustive search
problems.a: Relaxation followed by approximation (rounding)
problems.e: The LP relaxes integrality; randomized or deterministic rounding approximates an integer solution from it.

problems.q:
A hierarchical flow optimizes each block separately and then the top level with block abstracts. What is the main risk of this decomposition?

A) Decomposition always gives the global optimum

B) Interactions across block boundaries, such as cross-block timing, can be suboptimal or missed

C) Each block becomes NP-hard

D) The top level has no variables
problems.a: Interactions across block boundaries, such as cross-block timing, can be suboptimal or missed
problems.e: Decomposition is exact only when subproblems are independent; coupling must be handled by budgets or iteration.

problems.q:
A hierarchical flow optimizes each block separately and then the top level with block abstracts. What is the main risk of this decomposition?

A) The top level has no variables

B) Interactions across block boundaries, such as cross-block timing, can be suboptimal or missed

C) Each block becomes NP-hard

D) Decomposition always gives the global optimum
problems.a: Interactions across block boundaries, such as cross-block timing, can be suboptimal or missed
problems.e: Decomposition is exact only when subproblems are independent; coupling must be handled by budgets or iteration.

problems.q:
Min-cut placement recursively bisects the netlist and the die. Which strategy is this?

A) Penalty method

B) Decompose: split one big problem into many small ones

C) Relax integrality

D) Bayesian search
problems.a: Decompose: split one big problem into many small ones
problems.e: Recursive bisection is divide and conquer: each region becomes an independent smaller placement problem.

problems.q:
A team must solve 10^6-cell detailed placement in minutes and also wants a quality certificate. Which pairing fits?

A) Local search for the solution plus a relaxation bound to measure the gap

B) Exhaustive enumeration

C) Random placement with no bound

D) An ILP over all cells at once
problems.a: Local search for the solution plus a relaxation bound to measure the gap
problems.e: Search scales; a relaxation provides the bound that says how much quality might be left on the table.

problems.q:
Simulated annealing floorplanning perturbs a Polish expression and accepts or rejects. Which strategy is it?

A) Relaxation with an exact bound

B) Convex optimization

C) Search: explore the discrete space with moves and an acceptance rule

D) Benders decomposition
problems.a: Search: explore the discrete space with moves and an acceptance rule
problems.e: SA searches the space directly without bounds or relaxation, trading certificates for flexibility.

problems.q:
Which approach gives a lower bound on the optimum of a minimization problem?

A) Evaluating a random feasible point

B) Rounding a fractional solution

C) Running a heuristic search

D) Solving a relaxation
problems.a: Solving a relaxation
problems.e: Any feasible point gives an upper bound; a relaxation's optimum gives a lower bound. Together they bracket the optimum.

label: Linear programming and its geometry
lesson:
# Linear programming and its geometry

A linear program minimizes or maximizes a linear objective over a region cut out by linear inequalities. LPs sit inside EDA tools everywhere: linearized sizing and budgeting, clock-skew scheduling, LP relaxations of routing and covering ILPs, and the bounding step of every branch-and-bound solver. The geometry of two-variable LPs explains the whole theory: the feasible region is a convex polygon and an optimum, when one exists, sits at a corner.

## Vertices from tight constraints

Each inequality $a_i x + b_i y \le r_i$ is a half-plane, and the feasible region is their intersection with $x, y \ge 0$: a convex polygon. A vertex is a point where two boundary lines meet and every other constraint still holds. To find the vertex where constraints (1) and (2) are both tight, solve them as equations.

Take maximize $z = 6x + 5y$ subject to (1) $5x + 2y \le 22$ and (2) $x + 5y \le 9$. Solving $5x + 2y = 22$ and $x + 5y = 9$ gives $x = 4$, $y = 1$ (by elimination or Cramer's rule). The objective there is $6 \cdot 4 + 5 \cdot 1 = 29$. The other vertices come from the axes: $(0, 0)$, the x-intercept of the binding constraint $(4.4, 0)$, and the y-intercept $(0, 1.8)$.

## The optimum is at a vertex

A linear objective has parallel level lines $c_1 x + c_2 y = z$. Sliding the line in the improving direction, the last feasible point it touches is a vertex (or a whole edge, when the objective is parallel to it). So a bounded, feasible LP has an optimal vertex, and checking every vertex solves a small LP.

For the example above the vertices are $(0, 0)$ with $z = 0$, $(4.4, 0)$ with $z = 26.4$, $(4, 1)$ with $z = 29$, and $(0, 1.8)$ with $z = 9$. The optimum is 29 at $(4, 1)$. Changing the objective to $z = x + 10y$ moves it to $(0, 1.8)$ with $z = 18$: the region is fixed, the objective picks the corner. The simplex method walks from vertex to adjacent vertex, improving each step, and stops when no neighbour is better. Interior-point methods instead cross the inside of the region; both reach the same optimal value.

## Counting corners, redundancy and degeneracy

Adding a constraint can add a corner, remove corners, or change nothing. Add (3) $y \le 5$ to maximize subject to $3x + 2y \le 18$, $x + 3y \le 20$: the line $y = 5$ slices off the top, and the corners become $(0, 0)$, $(6, 0)$, $(8/3, 5)$ and $(0, 5)$, four in all. A constraint whose line never touches the region is redundant and adds no corner.

To count corners mechanically, intersect every pair of boundary lines (including the axes), keep the points that satisfy all constraints, and merge duplicates. Duplicates arise when three or more lines pass through the same point: degeneracy. Degenerate vertices are why simplex can pivot without moving, and why practical codes need anti-cycling rules. In EDA LPs with thousands of similar constraints, such as uniform track capacities, degeneracy is the norm, not the exception.

## Going deeper

Bertsimas and Tsitsiklis, "Introduction to Linear Optimization" (1997), chapters 1 to 3 on geometry and the simplex method; Chvatal, "Linear Programming" (1983), for degeneracy and cycling.

label: Standard form and the simplex pivot
lesson:
# Standard form and the simplex pivot

The simplex method is the algebra behind the vertex walk. It rewrites inequalities as equations with slack variables, represents a vertex as a basic solution, and moves to an adjacent vertex by a pivot that swaps one basic variable out and one nonbasic variable in. Every LP solver inside an EDA flow, and every branch-and-bound node of an ILP router, runs pivots like these, so the ratio test and reduced costs are worth knowing by hand.

## Standard form and basic solutions

Standard form writes $Ax \le b$ as $Ax + s = b$ with slacks $s \ge 0$. With $n$ original variables and $m$ inequality rows there are $n + m$ variables and $m$ equations. A basic solution chooses $m$ basic variables, sets the other $n$ to zero, and solves for the basics. When the basics are nonnegative the point is a vertex of the feasible region.

So a problem has at most $\binom{n + m}{m}$ basic solutions. A routing LP with 3 variables and 3 constraints has at most $\binom{6}{3} = 20$, and the count explodes for realistic sizes: $\binom{200}{100}$ is about $9 \times 10^{58}$. The simplex method is practical because it visits only a short sequence of improving bases, typically a small multiple of $m$ pivots, even though the worst case over specially built instances is exponential.

## The minimum-ratio test

A pivot raises one nonbasic variable, the entering variable, from zero. Each basic variable changes along the entering column: row $i$ has $x_{B_i} = b_i - a_i\theta$ where $a_i$ is the column coefficient and $\theta$ the entering value. Rows with $a_i \le 0$ never decrease, so they impose no limit. Rows with $a_i > 0$ hit zero at $\theta = b_i/a_i$. The entering variable rises to the smallest such ratio, and that row's basic variable leaves.

Example: column coefficients 2, 0, 4, 3 with right-hand sides 17, 19, 14, 8. The ratios for positive coefficients are 8.5, 3.5 and 2.67, so $\theta = 8/3 \approx 2.67$ and row 4's basic variable leaves the basis. If no coefficient is positive the entering variable can grow forever, and the LP is unbounded in that direction.

## Reduced costs and the objective step

A reduced cost $d_j$ says how much the objective changes per unit of nonbasic variable $x_j$ while the basics adjust to stay feasible. In a maximization, a positive reduced cost means $x_j$ is worth bringing in; when every reduced cost is nonpositive the current vertex is optimal.

After the pivot the objective changes by $d_j \theta$. Suppose the current objective is 16, $x_e$ has reduced cost 3, and its column has coefficients 4 and 4 in rows with right-hand sides 20 and 15. The ratio test gives $\theta = \min(20/4, 15/4) = 3.75$, and the new objective is $16 + 3 \cdot 3.75 = 27.25$. When the limiting ratio is zero (a degenerate vertex) the basis changes but the point and the objective do not. Pricing rules such as steepest edge choose the entering variable to cut the number of pivots.

## Going deeper

Bertsimas and Tsitsiklis, "Introduction to Linear Optimization" (1997), chapter 3; Vanderbei, "Linear Programming: Foundations and Extensions" (5th ed., 2020), for dictionaries and pivoting rules.

problems.e: Standard form has 3 + 3 = 6 variables and 3 equality rows. A basic solution picks 3 basic variables, so there are at most $\binom{6}{3} = 20$ of them. Simplex visits only a few, which is why it is fast in practice.

lesson:
# Linear programming duality

Every LP has a dual LP whose optimum equals the primal's. The dual is not a curiosity: its variables are prices on the primal's constraints, its feasible points are certificates that bound the primal, and its structure drives Lagrangian relaxation in gate sizing, Benders cuts, shadow prices on routing capacity and the stopping tests in every solver. Learning to write and use the dual is a core skill for reading EDA optimization papers.

## Weak duality gives bounds

For the primal maximize $c^T x$ subject to $Ax \le b$, $x \ge 0$, the dual is minimize $b^T y$ subject to $A^T y \ge c$, $y \ge 0$. One dual variable per primal constraint, one dual constraint per primal variable.

Weak duality: for any primal-feasible $x$ and dual-feasible $y$, $c^T x \le (A^T y)^T x = y^T A x \le y^T b$. So every dual-feasible point certifies an upper bound on the primal maximum. Take maximize $8x + 6y$ subject to $2x + 2y \le 18$ and $x + 6y \le 34$. The point $y_1 = 2$, $y_2 = 5$ satisfies $2y_1 + y_2 = 9 \ge 8$ and $2y_1 + 6y_2 = 34 \ge 6$, so it is dual feasible and certifies the bound $18 \cdot 2 + 34 \cdot 5 = 206$. A better dual point gives a tighter bound.

## Strong duality

Strong duality says that if the primal has a finite optimum, so does the dual, and the two optimal values are equal. No gap remains for LPs. So the dual optimum can be found by solving the primal, and vice versa.

For maximize $7x + 5y$ subject to $3x + y \le 16$ and $3x + 6y \le 21$, the vertices are $(0, 0)$, $(5.33, 0)$, $(5, 1)$ and $(0, 3.5)$, with objective values 0, 37.3, 40 and 17.5. The primal optimum is 40, so the dual minimum is 40 too. Solvers exploit this: a primal-dual pair with equal objectives proves optimality, which is how an LP code knows it can stop and how a test can check a solver's answer without trusting it. When the primal is unbounded the dual is infeasible, and the reverse case is also possible: the dual can be unbounded when the primal is infeasible.

## Optimal dual values at a vertex

At an optimal vertex the dual variables of the tight constraints solve $A_B^T y = c$, where $A_B$ holds the rows of the tight constraints, and slack constraints get $y = 0$. Nonnegative solutions confirm optimality: $c$ lies in the cone of the tight constraints' normals.

Example: maximize $6x + 5y$ subject to (1) $3x + y \le 7$ and (2) $3x + 4y \le 19$. The vertex $(1, 4)$ makes both tight. Solving $3y_1 + 3y_2 = 6$ and $y_1 + 4y_2 = 5$ gives $y_1 = 1$, $y_2 = 1$, both nonnegative, so $(1, 4)$ is optimal with $z = 26 = 7 \cdot 1 + 19 \cdot 1$. In Lagrangian-relaxation gate sizing the multipliers on timing arcs play exactly this role: they are the dual values of the timing constraints, and their optimality conditions become flow conservation on the timing graph.

## Going deeper

Bertsimas and Tsitsiklis, "Introduction to Linear Optimization" (1997), chapter 4; Chen, Chu and Wong, "Fast and exact simultaneous gate and wire sizing by Lagrangian relaxation" (IEEE TCAD, 1999), for duality applied to sizing.

label: Shadow prices and complementary slackness
lesson:
# Shadow prices and complementary slackness

A dual value is a price: how much the optimal objective improves per extra unit of a constraint's right-hand side. In EDA that is the value of one more routing track on an edge, one more unit of power budget, or one more picosecond on a path. Complementary slackness links primal and dual: a constraint with slack is worth nothing at the margin. Together these turn an LP solution into a sensitivity report that tells the designer where resources are binding.

## Slack at the optimum

The slack of constraint $i$ at a point is $r_i - a_i^T x$, the unused part of its right-hand side. At the optimum some constraints are tight (slack 0) and others are not.

Take maximize $7x + 11y$ subject to (1) $2x + 3y \le 11$, (2) $3x + 5y \le 18$, (3) $x \le 5$, with optimum $(1, 3)$. Constraint (1): $2 + 9 = 11$, slack 0. Constraint (2): $3 + 15 = 18$, slack 0. Constraint (3): $x = 1$ against 5, slack 4. Constraints (1) and (2) are binding; (3) is not. In a global-routing LP, the binding constraints are the edges whose capacity is fully used: the congestion bottlenecks. A non-binding constraint can move a little without changing the optimum, which is the first step of sensitivity analysis.

## Complementary slackness

Complementary slackness says that at optimal primal $x$ and dual $y$, for every constraint, $y_i \cdot \text{slack}_i = 0$, and for every variable, $x_j$ times its dual slack is 0. A constraint with positive slack has $y_i = 0$. A constraint with $y_i > 0$ is tight.

In the example, (3) has slack 4, so $y_3 = 0$. The tight constraints carry the duals: from $2y_1 + 3y_2 = 7$ and $3y_1 + 5y_2 = 11$ we get $y_1 = 2$, $y_2 = 1$. Check: $11 \cdot 2 + 18 \cdot 1 + 5 \cdot 0 = 40 = 7 \cdot 1 + 11 \cdot 3$, so primal and dual objectives agree. These conditions are the LP case of the KKT conditions, and in primal-dual interior-point methods they are the quantity driven to zero.

## Shadow prices and their range

The dual value $y_i$ is the shadow price of constraint $i$: raising $r_i$ by $\delta$ raises the optimum by $y_i \delta$, as long as the same constraints stay tight. In the LP above $y_1 = 2$. Raising $r_1$ from 11 to 11.5 moves the vertex to $(3.5, 1.5)$, and the optimum rises from 40 to 41, exactly $2 \cdot 0.5$.

The price holds only over a range. Raise $r_1$ to 12 and the same two tight constraints would put the vertex at $(6, 0)$, which violates $x \le 5$: constraint (3) becomes binding, the basis changes, and so does the price. Solvers report this range. For an EDA engineer the shadow price ranks investments: a routing edge with a large dual is the one where an extra track, a wider channel or a layer change pays most. A zero dual means that buying more of that resource does not help at all, however congested it looks.

## Going deeper

Bertsimas and Tsitsiklis, "Introduction to Linear Optimization" (1997), chapter 5 on sensitivity analysis; Vanderbei, "Linear Programming" (5th ed., 2020), chapter on duality and complementary slackness.

problems.q: A linearized budget LP allots x and y units of two resources to two blocks. Maximize $z = 24x + 21y$ subject to (1) $6x + y \le 40$, (2) $2x + 6y \le 36$, (3) $x \le 8$, and $x, y \ge 0$. The optimum is at $x = 6$, $y = 4$. What is the slack of constraint (3) at the optimum? Give an integer.
problems.e: Slack is right-hand side minus left-hand side at the optimum: 2. A constraint with positive slack is not binding.

label: Difference constraints and longest paths
lesson:
# Difference constraints and longest paths

A system of constraints $x_j - x_i \le w_{ij}$ is an LP with a special structure: it is the dual of a shortest-path problem, so it is solved by graph algorithms in place of a general LP solver. EDA uses it constantly: one-dimensional layout compaction, retiming feasibility, clock-skew scheduling and timing-budget distribution. Seeing the constraint graph behind such a system turns an LP into a Bellman-Ford or a longest-path pass.

## Compaction as a longest path

In one-dimensional compaction each layout edge has a position $x_i$, and design rules give minimum spacings $x_j \ge x_i + d_{ij}$. Build a graph with an edge $i \to j$ of weight $d_{ij}$ for each rule. The smallest feasible position of every element is its longest-path distance from the left boundary $x_0 = 0$, and on an acyclic graph that is one pass in topological order.

Example: $x_1 \ge x_0 + 6$, $x_2 \ge x_1 + 1$, $x_3 \ge x_2 + 2$, $x_3 \ge x_1 + 11$, $x_4 \ge x_3 + 3$, $x_4 \ge x_2 + 8$, $x_5 \ge x_4 + 4$. In order: $x_1 = 6$, $x_2 = 7$, $x_3 = \max(9, 17) = 17$, $x_4 = \max(20, 15) = 20$, $x_5 = 24$. The constraint achieving each maximum is the critical one; the chain $x_0, x_1, x_3, x_4, x_5$ fixes the width.

## Feasible solutions by shortest paths

For a general system $x_j - x_i \le w_{ij}$, weights may be negative and the graph may have cycles. Draw an edge $i \to j$ of weight $w_{ij}$ for each constraint and add a source $s$ with a zero-weight edge to every variable. Shortest-path distances $d$ satisfy $d_j \le d_i + w_{ij}$ for every edge, which is exactly the constraint, so $x = d$ is a feasible solution. Bellman-Ford computes it in $O(VE)$.

Example: $x_2 - x_4 \le -3$, $x_1 - x_2 \le 4$, $x_1 - x_4 \le -1$, $x_2 - x_1 \le -3$. Start every $x$ at 0. Relaxing gives $x_2 = -3$ (from $x_4 = 0$), $x_1 = -1$ (from $x_4$), then $x_2 = \min(-3, -1 - 3) = -4$, and nothing improves further: $x = (-1, -4, 0, 0)$. Any constant can be added to every variable and the system still holds.

## Negative cycles and the clock-skew bound

The system is infeasible exactly when the constraint graph has a negative cycle: summing the constraints around the cycle gives $0 \le$ a negative number. This is how clock-skew scheduling finds the best period.

With useful skew, flop $i$ gets clock arrival $s_i$, and a stage of delay $d_i$ into flop $i+1$ needs $s_i + d_i + t_{setup} \le s_{i+1} + T$, that is $s_i - s_{i+1} \le T - d_i - t_{setup}$. Around a loop of $k$ flops the skews cancel and feasibility needs $kT \ge \sum d_i + k\, t_{setup}$. For two flops with stage delays 890 ps and 630 ps and setup 10 ps, $T \ge 1520/2 + 10 = 770$ ps, though the slower stage alone would need 900 ps. Skew can balance a loop but never beat its average delay, so the optimal period is set by the maximum mean cycle of the timing graph.

## Going deeper

label: LP relaxation and the integrality gap
lesson:
# LP relaxation and the integrality gap

An integer program becomes an LP when its integrality requirements are dropped. That LP relaxation is the engine of every MILP solver: it bounds the optimum, guides branching and suggests roundings. In EDA, relaxations bound timing-repair selection, test compaction, global routing and floorplanning ILPs. The distance between the relaxed and the integer optimum, the integrality gap, measures how much work the solver still faces and how good a formulation is.

## Solving the relaxed knapsack

A repair pass choosing whole upsizes under an area budget is a 0-1 knapsack: maximize $\sum v_i x_i$ subject to $\sum w_i x_i \le W$, $x_i \in \{0, 1\}$, where $v_i$ is the TNS recovered and $w_i$ the area. Relax to $0 \le x_i \le 1$. The relaxed problem is solved greedily: sort by $v_i / w_i$, take items whole while they fit, then take the fraction of the next one that fills the budget.

Example: budget 14; upsize 1 recovers 23 ps for 7 units (3.29 ps per unit), upsize 3 recovers 7 ps for 5 units (1.4), upsize 2 recovers 5 ps for 12 units (0.42). Take upsize 1 (7 units left), then upsize 3 (2 units left), then $2/12$ of upsize 2: $23 + 7 + 5 \cdot 2/12 = 30.83$ ps. Only one variable ends fractional, a general property of LP vertices with one coupling constraint.

## The integer optimum

The integer optimum must pick whole items. For small instances enumerate the feasible subsets; for large ones a solver branches. In the example the subsets that fit in 14 units are $\{1, 3\}$ worth 30, $\{1\}$ worth 23, $\{2\}$ worth 5, $\{3\}$ worth 7, and the empty set. $\{1, 2\}$ needs 19 units and $\{2, 3\}$ needs 17, so both are infeasible. The integer optimum is 30 ps.

The relaxation bound, 30.83, is never below the integer optimum for a maximization, because every integer solution is also feasible for the LP. A bound is only useful if it is tight. Greedy by ratio is not optimal for the integer problem in general: an item with a lower ratio can pack the budget better, which is why rounding the LP is a heuristic and branch and bound is needed for proof.

## Integrality gap and formulation strength

The integrality gap of an instance is the relaxed optimum minus the integer optimum (or their ratio). Here it is $30.83 - 30 = 0.83$ ps. A small gap means the LP nearly describes the integer hull and branch and bound will prune quickly. A large gap means many nodes.

Formulations of the same problem can have very different gaps. Big-M disjunctions for floorplan non-overlap are notoriously weak: the LP can set binaries to tiny fractions and ignore overlap entirely. Adding valid inequalities (cuts), using tighter M values, or reformulating with more variables (for example, path or pattern variables in routing and covering) shrinks the gap. A useful habit when building an EDA ILP is to solve the relaxation of a small instance first and compare: the gap predicts how the model will scale long before the full run does.

## Going deeper

Wolsey, "Integer Programming" (2nd ed., 2020), chapters 1 and 2 on formulations and relaxations; Martello and Toth, "Knapsack Problems" (1990).

label: Integer programming and branch and bound
prereqs: LP relaxation and the integrality gap
lesson:
# Integer programming and branch and bound

Branch and bound solves integer programs exactly by building a tree: each node is a subproblem with some variables fixed, its relaxation gives a bound, and any node whose bound cannot beat the best known solution is pruned. It is the core of every MILP solver used for EDA ILPs, and the same bound-and-prune idea drives exact covering, ATPG search (PODEM backtracks over input assignments) and exact floorplanning. Understanding pruning and gaps is how you read a solver log.

## Pruning by bound

Keep an incumbent, the best feasible integer solution found so far. Each open node carries a bound from its relaxation. For maximization the bound is an upper bound on any solution in that subtree; if it is at most the incumbent, the subtree cannot contain a strictly better solution and is pruned. For minimization the test flips: prune when the lower bound is at least the incumbent.

Example: a covering search for a minimum test set has an incumbent of 48 patterns and open nodes with lower bounds 50, 51, 52, 52, 46 and 49. Every node with bound at least 48 is pruned: 50, 51, 52, 52 and 49, five nodes. Only the node with bound 46 might hold a 46- or 47-pattern cover. A node is also pruned when its relaxation is infeasible, and when its relaxed solution is integral, in which case it may become the new incumbent.

## Branching on a fractional variable

When a node's relaxation has a fractional variable $x_k = f$, branch: one child adds $x_k \le \lfloor f \rfloor$, the other $x_k \ge \lceil f \rceil$; for binaries, $x_k = 0$ and $x_k = 1$. Each child's relaxation is solved, and its bound is never better than the parent's.

In the knapsack example (budget 14; upsizes worth 23, 5, 7 ps for 7, 12, 5 units) the root LP is 30.83 with $x_2 = 1/6$ fractional. Child $x_2 = 0$: the greedy LP over items 1 and 3 takes both whole, bound 30, and the solution is integral, so it becomes the incumbent. Child $x_2 = 1$: 12 units used, 2 left, take $2/7$ of upsize 1: $5 + 23 \cdot 2/7 = 11.57$. That is below the incumbent 30, so it is pruned. The search ends after three nodes. Branching on the most fractional variable is common, but strong branching, which tests several candidates, usually shrinks the tree more.

## Reading the optimality gap

At any moment the best bound over all open nodes and the incumbent bracket the optimum. Solvers report the relative gap, commonly $(\text{bound} - \text{incumbent})/|\text{incumbent}|$ for maximization (definitions vary slightly between solvers). A MILP global router with incumbent 547 and best bound 594 has gap $47/547 = 8.59\%$: no solution can be more than 8.59% better than the one in hand.

The gap is the certificate EDA flows use to stop early: a floorplanner may accept 1% and save most of the run time, since closing the last fraction of a gap often costs more than finding the first good solution. Two forces close it: better incumbents from heuristics (diving, rounding, local search) and better bounds from cuts and branching. A gap that stalls with the incumbent fixed is a sign of a weak relaxation, not of a bad heuristic.

## Going deeper

label: Big-M and disjunctive constraints
prereqs: LP relaxation and the integrality gap
Logical connectives: AND, OR, NOT, IMPLIES
lesson:
# Big-M and disjunctive constraints

Many EDA rules are either-or: block i is left of, right of, below or above block j; a cell sits in one of two regions; a wire uses one of two layers. Integer programs encode such disjunctions with binaries and a large constant M that switches a constraint off. Big-M models are easy to write and are how ILP floorplanners and legalizers are usually stated, but a careless M ruins the relaxation, so choosing the smallest valid M is a real skill.

## Choosing the smallest valid M

The constraint $x_i + w_i \le x_j + Mp$ forces block i left of block j when $p = 0$ and must be vacuous when $p = 1$. Vacuous means it holds for every feasible placement, so M must cover the worst case: $M \ge \max (x_i + w_i - x_j)$ over the allowed ranges. That maximum is at the largest $x_i$ and the smallest $x_j$.

Example: block i is 21 um wide with fence $0 \le x_i \le 70$, and block j's fence requires $x_j \ge 2$. Then $M \ge 70 + 21 - 2 = 89$ um. Any larger M is still valid, but each extra unit loosens the LP relaxation. With no fences, on a chip of width W, the bound is W. Deriving M from the actual variable bounds, region by region, is cheap and often halves solve times.

## Counting binaries in disjunctive models

Pairwise non-overlap for n rectangles needs one disjunction per pair. A standard encoding uses two binaries $(p_{ij}, q_{ij})$ per pair to pick one of four relations, left-of, right-of, below or above, with four big-M constraints of which three are switched off. There are $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs, so $2\binom{n}{2} = n(n-1)$ binaries.

For 8 blocks that is 28 pairs and 56 binaries; with a rotation binary per block, $56 + 8 = 64$. For 50 blocks it is 2450 binaries, plus 4900 big-M constraints. The count grows quadratically, and every pair's binaries interact through the coordinates, so the tree grows fast. Exact ILP floorplanning is therefore practical only for small block counts, and larger floorplanners use sequence pairs or Polish expressions with annealing, or fix relative orders from a constraint graph and solve an LP for the coordinates.

## Why big-M relaxations are weak

In the LP relaxation $p$ may be fractional, and a small fraction of a large M buys a large violation. Take $w_i = 38$ um, $M = 350$ um, $x_i = 50$, $x_j = 80$: the blocks overlap by $50 + 38 - 80 = 8$ um, yet $p = 8/350 = 0.023$ satisfies the relaxed constraint. The LP pays almost nothing to ignore non-overlap, so its bound is close to the bound with no non-overlap constraints at all.

The remedies are the standard ones: the smallest valid M, symmetry breaking (fix the relative order of identical blocks), valid inequalities that link the binaries to the block dimensions and the die size, and, best of all, a different formulation. Indicator constraints, which solvers branch on directly, avoid M entirely. Fixing the relative-position binaries from a heuristic and then solving the LP for coordinates is how many legalizers use this model in practice.

## Going deeper

Sutanthavibul, Shragowitz and Rosen, "An analytical approach to floorplan design and optimization" (IEEE TCAD, 1991), the classic MILP floorplanning model; Wolsey, "Integer Programming" (2nd ed., 2020), chapter 1 on formulations.

label: ILP formulation of operation scheduling
prereqs: LP relaxation and the integrality gap
lesson:
# ILP formulation of operation scheduling

High-level synthesis must assign operations of a dataflow graph to control steps so that dependences hold and the number of functional units stays within a limit. The textbook exact method is a time-indexed integer program. Its size, and therefore its solve time, is governed by each operation's mobility window, and its resource constraints decide how many adders and multipliers the datapath needs. The same template schedules tests, tasks on an accelerator, and cuts in a lithography flow.

## Time-indexed binaries and their count

Let $x_{i,t} = 1$ when operation i starts in step t. Each operation starts exactly once: $\sum_t x_{i,t} = 1$. Its start time is $\sum_t t\, x_{i,t}$, so a dependence $i \to j$ with delay $d_i$ is linear: $\sum_t t\, x_{j,t} \ge \sum_t t\, x_{i,t} + d_i$.

Variables only need to exist where an operation can actually start, between its ASAP and ALAP times. With windows op1 [3, 5], op2 [3, 8], op3 [7, 8], op4 [7, 8], op5 [2, 3] and op6 [3, 4], the counts are 3, 6, 2, 2, 2 and 2, total 17 binaries, against $6 \times 8 = 48$ without pruning. Window pruning is the cheapest and most effective model reduction in ILP scheduling, and tighter latency bounds shrink windows further.

## ASAP, ALAP and mobility

ASAP times come from a forward longest-path pass: sources start in step 1, and each operation starts one step (its delay) after its latest predecessor. ALAP times come from a backward pass under the latency bound L: sinks start at L, and each operation must start before its earliest successor. Mobility is ALAP minus ASAP.

Example with single-cycle operations and dependences op1 to op2, op1 to op3, op2 to op4, op1 to op5, op4 to op5, op5 to op6, and $L = 5$. ASAP: op1 = 1, op2 = 2, op3 = 2, op4 = 3, op5 = 4, op6 = 5. ALAP: op6 = 5, op5 = 4, op4 = 3, op2 = 2, op1 = 1, and op3 has no successor so it may wait until 5. Op4 has mobility 0: it is on the critical path. Op3 has mobility 3 and four candidate steps.

## Resource constraints and unit counts

Resource limits are linear in the binaries. An operation of type r with delay $d_i$ is busy in step t if it started in any of the $d_i$ steps up to t, so the constraint for each step and type is $\sum_{i \in r} \sum_{\tau = t - d_i + 1}^{t} x_{i,\tau} \le a_r$.

Given a schedule, the smallest $a_r$ it satisfies is the peak number of busy units. Multiplier mul1 starts in step 3 for 3 steps (busy in 3, 4, 5), mul2 starts in 2 for 2 steps (2, 3), mul3 starts in 2 for 1 step (2), and mul4 starts in 4 for 3 steps (4, 5, 6). Busy counts: step 2 has 2, step 3 has 2, step 4 has 2, step 5 has 2, step 6 has 1, so 2 multipliers suffice. Making $a_r$ a variable with a cost turns the ILP into the area-latency trade-off that HLS tools explore, and list scheduling is the fast heuristic that approximates it.

## Going deeper

Hwang, Lee and Hsu, "A formal approach to the scheduling problem in high level synthesis" (IEEE TCAD, 1991); De Micheli, "Synthesis and Optimization of Digital Circuits" (1994), chapter 5.

label: Global routing as an integer program
prereqs: LP relaxation and the integrality gap
Expectation of a function of a random variable
lesson:
# Global routing as an integer program

Global routing assigns each net a route through a coarse grid of routing regions so that no edge carries more wires than its capacity and total wirelength stays small. Written as an integer program, each net picks one candidate route, and edge capacities couple the nets. Routers built on this model solve its LP relaxation and round, and the same model underlies negotiated-congestion routers that price overflow. It is the cleanest example of relaxation plus rounding in physical design.

## Usage, capacity and overflow

Give each net n a set of candidate routes, and a binary $x_{n,r}$ that selects route r. Each net takes one: $\sum_r x_{n,r} = 1$. Edge e has usage $u_e = \sum_{(n,r) \ni e} x_{n,r}$ and capacity $c_e$. The overflow is $\sum_e \max(0, u_e - c_e)$.

Example: capacities e1 = 1, e2 = 1, e3 = 2, e4 = 1, e5 = 1. Net 1 takes e1, e2, e4; net 2 takes e2, e4, e5; net 3 takes e4. Usage: e1 = 1, e2 = 2, e3 = 0, e4 = 3, e5 = 1. Overflow: e2 has 1 excess and e4 has 2, total 3. Routers report total overflow and the maximum overflow per edge, because a few badly overflowed edges are much harder to fix in detailed routing than many slightly full ones.

## The 0-1 routing program

The exact model minimizes total wirelength $\sum_{n,r} \ell_{n,r} x_{n,r}$ subject to one route per net and $u_e \le c_e$ on every edge. With 3 nets and 2 candidates each there are $2^3 = 8$ assignments, few enough to check by hand: compute each assignment's usage, discard those that overflow, and keep the shortest.

Real instances have millions of nets and implicit candidate sets (all paths in the grid), so routers generate candidates on demand by shortest-path searches, which is column generation in LP terms. When the capacities cannot all be met, the objective weights overflow heavily and the result tells the placer where to spread cells. Pricing edges by their congestion and rerouting nets repeatedly, as negotiated-congestion routers do, is a heuristic for this same program.

## LP relaxation and randomized rounding

Relax each $x_{n,r}$ to $[0, 1]$. The LP spreads a net over several routes, for example net 1 with 0.2 on route A and 0.8 on route B. Randomized rounding then picks route A with probability 0.2 and route B with 0.8, independently per net.

By linearity of expectation the expected usage of an edge equals its LP usage: the sum of the fractional weights of the routes that cross it. If e2 is crossed by net 1's route A (0.2), net 2's route A (0.1) and net 3's route B (0.3), its expected usage is $0.2 + 0.1 + 0.3 = 0.6$. Because the LP respects capacities, rounding respects them in expectation, and Chernoff bounds show that overflow beyond a logarithmic factor is unlikely, which is the classic analysis of Raghavan and Thompson. In practice routers round, then repair the remaining overflow by rip-up and reroute.

## Going deeper

Raghavan and Thompson, "Randomized rounding: a technique for provably good algorithms and algorithmic proofs" (Combinatorica, 1987); McMurchie and Ebeling, "PathFinder: a negotiation-based performance-driven router for FPGAs" (FPGA, 1995); the OpenROAD documentation for its global router.

label: Cutting planes and branch and cut
prereqs: Integer programming and branch and bound
LP relaxation and the integrality gap
lesson:
# Cutting planes and branch and cut

A cutting plane is an inequality that every integer solution satisfies but the current LP solution violates. Adding it shrinks the relaxation toward the integer hull without losing any integer point, so bounds improve and the branch-and-bound tree shrinks. Modern MILP solvers are branch-and-cut codes, and knapsack-like rows from legalization, covering and capacity constraints in EDA models are exactly where cover cuts and Chvatal-Gomory cuts earn their keep.

## Cover inequalities

For a binary knapsack row $\sum a_i x_i \le b$, a cover is a set C whose weights sum to more than b. No feasible integer point can set every variable in C to 1, so $\sum_{i \in C} x_i \le |C| - 1$ is valid.

Example: $4x_1 + 8x_2 + 5x_3 + 2x_4 \le 12$. The set $\{x_2, x_3\}$ weighs 13, more than 12, so it is a cover and $x_2 + x_3 \le 1$ holds for every integer solution. The LP point $x = (0.2, 0.9, 0.2, 1)$ satisfies the knapsack row ($0.8 + 7.2 + 1 + 2 = 11$) but has $x_2 + x_3 = 1.1$, violating the cut by 0.1. Adding the cut removes this fractional point. Minimal covers, where dropping any item leaves a non-cover, give the strongest cuts, and lifting extends them to variables outside the cover.

## Chvatal-Gomory rounding

For nonnegative integer variables, any valid inequality can be strengthened by scaling and rounding. Multiply $5x + 6y \le 14$ by $u = 1/3$: $1.667x + 2y \le 4.667$. Rounding the left coefficients down keeps the inequality valid because $x, y \ge 0$: $x + 2y \le 4.667$. Now the left side is an integer for integer x and y, so the right side can be rounded down too: $x + 2y \le 4$.

That is a Chvatal-Gomory cut. It is valid for every integer point but can cut off fractional ones, such as $x = 0$, $y = 2.33$ allowed by the original row. Gomory's fractional cuts, generated from a row of the optimal simplex tableau, are a special case, and every valid inequality for a pure integer program can be obtained by repeating this procedure finitely often, although in practice solvers add only a few rounds.

## Validity and branch and cut

A cut must never remove a feasible integer point. Checking a proposed cut on a small instance is direct: enumerate the integer points that satisfy the constraints and count those that violate the cut. For $5x + 2y \le 8$ with $0 \le x, y \le 3$, the feasible points are $(0,0)$ to $(0,3)$, $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$, six in all, and none has $x + y > 4$, so $x + y \le 4$ is valid; it is also useless, since no LP point violates it either. A cut is only worth adding if it is both valid and violated.

Branch and cut adds violated cuts at the root and at nodes, re-solves the LP, and branches when cuts stop helping. The trade-off is LP size versus bound quality, so solvers manage a cut pool and drop inactive cuts. Cuts derived from problem structure, such as capacity cuts in routing, often beat generic ones.

## Going deeper

Wolsey, "Integer Programming" (2nd ed., 2020), chapters 8 and 9; Nemhauser and Wolsey, "Integer and Combinatorial Optimization" (1988), for cover inequalities and Chvatal-Gomory closure.

problems.q: A binary knapsack row from a placement-legalization ILP reads $7x_1 + 3x_2 + 3x_3 + 3x_4 + 6x_5 \le 15$. The LP relaxation returns $x_1 = 0.5$, $x_2 = 0$, $x_3 = 0.8$, $x_4 = 0.7$, $x_5 = 0.9$. The set {x_1, x_3, x_5} is a cover (its weights exceed 15), giving the cover inequality $x_1 + x_3 + x_5 \le 2$. By how much does the LP point violate it? Round to 2 decimal places.

label: Benders decomposition
prereqs: Integer programming and branch and bound
lesson:
# Benders decomposition

Benders decomposition splits a mixed-integer program into a master problem over the complicating integer variables and an LP subproblem over the continuous rest. The subproblem's dual returns cuts that teach the master about the continuous part. It suits EDA models with discrete structural choices and many continuous details, such as macro positions with wire flows, or buffer locations with timing LPs, and it is the formal version of fix-the-structure-then-optimize-the-details loops tools already run.

## Master and subproblem

Write the problem as minimize $f^T y + c^T x$ subject to $Wx \ge h - Gy$, $x \ge 0$, y integer. The integer y couples everything; for fixed y the rest is an LP in x. Benders keeps y in a master problem and replaces the LP by an auxiliary variable $\theta$ that underestimates its optimal cost.

The master solves minimize $f^T y + \theta$ subject to the cuts found so far. For its proposed $y$, the subproblem LP is solved. If it is infeasible, an extreme ray of its dual yields a feasibility cut excluding that y and others like it. If it is feasible, its optimal dual gives an optimality cut. When the continuous part splits into independent blocks, such as one routing region each, the subproblem becomes many small LPs solved in parallel, each returning its own cut. Benders partitions variables; Lagrangian relaxation instead dualizes the coupling constraints.

## Evaluating an optimality cut

By LP duality the subproblem cost for fixed y is $\max\{u^T(h - Gy) : W^T u \le c, u \ge 0\}$. Any dual-feasible u therefore gives a lower bound valid for every y: $\theta \ge u^T(h - Gy)$. The optimal u at the current y makes the bound tight there.

Example: $h = (5, 13)$, $G = (1, 4)^T$ with a scalar y, and an earlier subproblem returned $u = (0, 3)$. At $y = 1$ the cut says $\theta \ge 0 \cdot (5 - 1) + 3 \cdot (13 - 4) = 27$. At $y = 2$ it says $\theta \ge 3 \cdot (13 - 8) = 15$. Each cut is a linear function of y, so the master's view of the subproblem cost is the maximum of all cuts: a piecewise-linear underestimate that improves with every iteration. The common slips are adding $Gy$ instead of subtracting it and dropping a dual component.

## Bounds, convergence and fit

Each iteration gives two bounds for a minimization. The master's optimum, with only some cuts, is a lower bound. The master's y evaluated exactly, $f^T y$ plus the subproblem cost, is an upper bound. Stop when they meet within a tolerance: lower bound 812 and upper bound 830 put the best solution within $18/812 \approx 2.2\%$ of optimal.

Convergence can be slow, because each cut may raise the lower bound a little and the master, an integer program, is re-solved with more rows every time. Remedies include stronger (Pareto-optimal) cuts, several cuts per iteration, and branch-and-Benders-cut, which adds cuts inside one search tree instead of restarting. Benders is a poor fit when fixing the integers does not leave an easy, decomposable continuous part.

## Going deeper

Benders, "Partitioning procedures for solving mixed-variables programming problems" (Numerische Mathematik, 1962); Rahmaniani, Crainic, Gendreau and Rei, "The Benders decomposition algorithm: a literature review" (European Journal of Operational Research, 2017).

problems.q:
Which variables are the natural master-problem variables in a Benders decomposition of a floorplan-plus-routing model?

A) The continuous wire flows

B) The dual variables of capacity rows

C) The objective coefficients

D) The complicating integer decisions, such as block positions or relative orders
problems.a: The complicating integer decisions, such as block positions or relative orders
problems.e: Benders keeps the complicating (usually integer) variables in the master; fixing them leaves an easy LP in the continuous rest.

problems.q:
How does Benders differ from Lagrangian relaxation in what it decomposes?

A) Benders partitions the variables; Lagrangian relaxation dualizes the coupling constraints

B) Benders dualizes constraints and Lagrangian relaxation partitions variables

C) They are the same method

D) Benders never uses duality
problems.a: Benders partitions the variables; Lagrangian relaxation dualizes the coupling constraints
problems.e: Benders fixes complicating variables (row generation in the master); Lagrangian relaxation prices complicating constraints into the objective.

problems.q:
What does the master's auxiliary variable $\theta$ represent?

A) An underestimate of the subproblem's optimal cost as a function of the master variables

B) The number of cuts so far

C) The integer part of the objective

D) The duality gap
problems.a: An underestimate of the subproblem's optimal cost as a function of the master variables
problems.e: Optimality cuts bound $\theta$ from below; at convergence $\theta$ equals the true subproblem cost at the master's choice.

problems.q:
In a Benders scheme the master problem picks an integer macro decision y; the LP subproblem $\min\{c^T x : Wx \ge h - Gy\}$ has right-hand side $h = (6, 20)$ and $G = (1, 3)^T$. At an earlier master point the subproblem dual returned $u = (2, 1)$, giving the optimality cut $\theta \ge u^T(h - Gy)$. What lower bound does this cut put on $\theta$ at $y = 0$?

A) 31

B) 32

C) 20

D) 33
problems.e: Evaluate $u^T(h - Gy) = 2(6 - 1 \cdot 0) + 1(20 - 3 \cdot 0) = 32$. Any dual-feasible u gives a valid bound for every y by weak duality.

A) 63

B) -3

C) -12

D) 129
problems.e: Evaluate $u^T(h - Gy) = 3(9 - 2 \cdot 3) + 4(9 - 4 \cdot 3) = -3$. Any dual-feasible u gives a valid bound for every y by weak duality.

At an earlier master point the subproblem dual returned $u = (4, 4)$, giving the optimality cut $\theta \ge u^T(h - Gy)$. What lower bound does this cut put on $\theta$ at $y = 2$?

A) 96

B) -4

C) 64

D) 32
problems.e: Evaluate $u^T(h - Gy) = 4(11 - 1 \cdot 2) + 4(5 - 3 \cdot 2) = 32$. Any dual-feasible u gives a valid bound for every y by weak duality.

Benders on a large MILP converges slowly with the lower bound creeping up by tiny amounts. Which is a standard remedy?

A) Drop the subproblem

B) Add stronger cuts (for example Pareto-optimal cuts) or several cuts per iteration

C) Increase the annealing temperature

D) Remove the master variables
problems.a: Add stronger cuts (for example Pareto-optimal cuts) or several cuts per iteration
problems.e: Cut quality drives convergence; strengthened or multi-cuts tighten the master faster.

When is Benders decomposition a poor fit?

A) When fixing the integer variables does not leave an easy, decomposable continuous part

B) When the subproblem is an LP

C) When the problem has a linear objective

D) When there are integer variables
problems.a: When fixing the integer variables does not leave an easy, decomposable continuous part
problems.e: Benders pays off only if the residual problem is much easier than the whole; otherwise the cuts cost more than they save.

B) Remove the master variables

C) Increase the annealing temperature

D) Drop the subproblem
problems.a: Add stronger cuts (for example Pareto-optimal cuts) or several cuts per iteration
